description:
Team Concinendial is a small team that cares about two things: getting space history right, and making it easy for anyone to explore.

 Uiyun(Ian): Team Leader |Designed the animation, general architecture and the 3D scenes

Semin : Managing Head | Runs the project and the story and shaped the narrative around what NASA left behind

 Junyi : Advisor for User Experience| Shaped the Flight School tutorial, tested readability, and designed how visitors move from the intro to free exploration.
summary:
Most of the machines NASA sent into space never came home. Surveyor 3 sits on the Moon, Spirit is parked on Mars, and the Voyager probes are still flying. But if you’re 12 and want their stories, you end up in catalogues and PDFs.

So we built Since 1958, a time machine that opens in any browser. Press play and the Solar System runs from 1958 to today, with the planets and the Moon where they really were. Each machine shows up on the day it arrived, at its real coordinates. You can watch it land, walk up to it in real gravity, take it apart in 3D, or ride along with the Voyagers. Every object tells you why it was sent, what it found and why it stayed.

We checked dates, coordinates and facts against NASA’s NSSDCA catalogue, LROC images and mission pages, and every object lists its sources. Anything we simplified, like probe flight paths, is labelled in the app. It’s free, needs no account, and covers 13 sites on the Moon, 11 on Mars and 11 probes in deep space. A story you can walk through.

Most of them are silent. Their achievements are not.
details: Since 1958 is a 3D website that works like a time machine for the machines NASA left behind. You start in 1958, press play, and watch NASA's spacecraft land on the Moon and Mars or head into deep space, each on its real date and at its real spot. Once something has landed, you can fly down to it, walk around the Apollo sites in the Moon's real gravity, pull the hardware apart in 3D, and find out what it was built for, what it discovered and why it never came back. The story is about what stays behind. The opening counts every machine left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. On the timeline, each one goes quiet on the real day it fell silent. Every object answers the same questions: why it was sent, what it found, and why it stayed. The four longer animations each end with what that mission left behind: Apollo 11's descent stage and the laser mirror that still answers us, Perseverance's heat shield, sky crane and ten sealed sample tubes, Voyager 1 heading out of the Solar System for good, and James Webb, which will stay at L2 when its fuel runs out. Our motto sums it up: they are silent, but their achievements are not. There's a lot in it: 24 sites on the Moon and Mars, 11 spacecraft in deep space, 83 events on the timeline, 30 short mission films, four longer animations and a virtual exhibition hall where you can walk past every machine side by side. One of our favourite parts is the Voyager message. In 2017 NASA received more than 30,000 messages for Voyager 1, so we let you write one too and watch a simulated signal travel out at the speed of light. Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026, and the site uses its real distance. We made it for students and anyone curious about space, roughly age 10 and up. When we started researching, we found that most information about old missions is buried in technical pages. Hardly anyone knows that Surveyor 3 is still sitting on the Moon, or what Spirit actually found before it got stuck. Our goal was one place where you can see all of it and connect each machine to what we learned because of it. It runs in a web browser, on a laptop or a phone, with nothing to install and no account, and a hands-on tutorial gets you started. Getting the facts right mattered a lot to us. Dates, landing coordinates and facts come from NASA's NSSDCA catalogue and NASA mission pages, and every object lists its sources. Planet positions are calculated with Astronomy Engine, and most of the 3D models come from NASA 3D Resources. Where NASA didn't have a model, we built one ourselves to the real size. A "What is real?" panel is honest about what we simplified, like the paths probes take between planets.
